newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Mercosur spat hasn't put off investors - Argentina.
newsitem.headline: Mercosur spat hasn't put off investors - Argentina.

text.p: A trade spat in South America's Mercosur customs union over Brazilian import moves has not put off foreign investors interested in the region, Argentine Economy Minister Roque Fernandez said Monday.

Fernandez, who attended a weekend summit with Argentine President Carlos Menem and Brazil's Fernando Henrique Cardoso, stressed the "true vocation for economic integration" between Mercosur members Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay.

That vocation has been put to the test by Brazil's recent decision to combat its yawning trade gap by putting new limits on import financing of less than 360 days, effectively forcing importers to pay in cash.

Brazil's Mercosur partners immediately howled that the measures were "protectionist" and they had not been warned, prompting Brazil to tone down the rules for Mercosur until July 31, while long-term solutions are sought.
But Fernandez told foreign correspondents that in no way was any Mercosur member's commitment to integration in doubt.

"That's the most important thing for foreign investors, who clearly understand this because we've seen no stop in the flow of foreign investment as a consequence of this problem or previous problems," the minister said.

Fernandez said investors could tell that unilateral moves like Brazil's import financing limits, which triggered the row, "are measures produced by specific circumstances, based on one country's political and macroeconomic needs, rather than ideas that go against economic integration in Mercosur."

Fernandez told one paper the outcome of the Rio de Janeiro summit between Menem and Cardoso was "not great, but the best that was possible." Menem failed to get Brazil to reverse the import moves but said Brazil agreed to give Mercosur partners advance warning of such moves in future to "avoid surprises."
He also clinched a deal allowing carmakers in Argentina to export 110,000 vehicles to Brazil in the next three years.

Fernandez said such meetings were "not an arm-wrestle" and that he had some sympathies with Brazil's argument that it put controls on import financing to stop speculation which acted "as an artificial incentive which distorts trade."
